newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. says its Rwanda war crimes tribunal mismanaged.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says its Rwanda war crimes tribunal mismanaged.

text.p: Two years after its creation, the Rwanda war crimes tribunal suffers from mismanagement, unqualified staff and neglect from New York headquarters, according to a new U.N. investigation.

The report, released on Wednesday, sets out in detail financial abuses and mismangement in the administrative aparatus as well as apparent legal chaos in the prosecutor's office set up to investigate the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.

Some of the complaints emerged several months ago and both Secretary-General Kofi Annan and his predecessor Boutros Boutros-Ghali have made key personnel changes. But the report called for further "substantial" changes.

Otherwise "the Rwandese will be right to suspect that justice delayed is justice denied," said the report by Karl Paschke, the U.N.'s equivalent of an inspector-general, who heads the Office of Internal Oversight Services.
He said "serious operational deficiencies in the management of the tribunal" had developed virtually from its 1995 inception to the time of the investigation in November.
Set up in Arusha, Tanzania, the tribunal is to try leaders responsible for more than half a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus massacred in Rwanda in 1994 by Hutu troops and others.
A sub-office for prosecutors and investigators is located in the Rwandan capital of Kigali. The split in locations Paschke said had contributed distrust and misunderstandings.

The tribunal has indicted 21 people. The first trial is currently underway against Jean-Paul Akayesu, 43, the former mayor of Rwanda's Taba commune, charged with inciting the public to slaughter and ordering killings.

In the Arusha registrar's office, headed by Andronico Adede of Kenya, Pashke said that "not a single administrative area" functioned effectively. There was no accounting system, budgets were haphazard and staff in key jobs were unqualified.

One employee received a double salary, kept silent about it, asked for an advance and still owes the United Nations more than $34,000. Yet his contract was extended until mid-1997, with the approval of the U.N. personnel department.

In another instance a plane costing $27,000 went to pick up suspects in a West Africa country, presumably Cameroon, but it left empty because of no prior agreement with that country for the surrender of the prisoners, the report said.
Cameroon in January finally did hand over four suspects, including Col. Theoneste Bagosora, described as giving military orders at the beginning of the 1994 massacres.

Paschke said that the prosecutor's office in Kigali, headed by deputy prosecutor Honoure Rakotomanana of Madagascar, suffered from inexperienced staff, a lack of vehicles, computers, office equipment and appalling security conditions,
The prosecutor, first Richard Goldstone of South Africa, now Louise Arbor of Canada, serves as chief prosecutor for the Hague-based tribunal on the former Yugoslavia also.
Goldstone's instructions to concentrate indictments on national figures first were ignored and various legal staff followed their own strategies at will, the report said.

But Paschke said many of the tasks had to be performed without support or resources from New York, particularly the departments of legal affairs headed by Hans Corell of Sweden and administration and management, headed by Joseph Connor of the United States.

The U.N. secretariat, he said, believed erroneously the tribunal was independent. "The evidence suggests that once a few key administrators were selected, the secretariat failed to take responsibiity to provide essential support for the tribunal until it could become functional," he said.
